title: Nachiketa and the worn-out cows
hookLine: a boy watches his father give away worn-out cows, and asks one question too many
tomorrow: three nights at Death's door, and nobody brings him water

cards: A charity drive at a big house. The owner is making a show of generosity, and his servants lead the gifts out one by one. But the kid in the doorway notices something.
The gifts are the old stuff: cows that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and will never calf again. Everyone else nods politely. The boy can't.
So begins the Katha Upanishad: a boy named Nachiketa, a father's careless gift, and, before long, Death.

teach.b: The father, Vajashravasa, is performing a sacrifice where you're meant to give away everything you own. But his cows are worn out.
The text says it bluntly: they've drunk their water, eaten their grass, been milked dry, and will bear no more. Joyless worlds, it says, await the one who gives gifts like these.
Then: shraddha entered the boy. Shraddha is faith, trust, a deep seriousness; you met it in the Gita. It enters Nachiketa, still a child, and he goes to his father.

teach.h: TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?
teach.b: Father, to whom will you give me? If the sacrifice means giving everything, the son belongs on the list. It's a real question, and a sharp one.
The father doesn't answer. Nachiketa asks a second time, then a third.
And the father, angry, the way a parent can be when a child sees through them in front of others, snaps: I give you to Death. To Yama. It's an ancient story, and a very modern one.
A parent says something in anger they can't take back, and a child takes them at their word.
Nachiketa doesn't run and hide. He thinks it through: I go first among many, in the middle of many. What will Yama do with me?
He sees that people ripen and fall like grain, and rise again like grain. And he goes. Here's the first teaching of the week, and Hindus still live by it.
An offering without shraddha is empty. The ritual was done, the cows were counted, and the text still calls those gifts joyless.
That's why, in puja, families give God the fresh fruit and the whole flower, never the leftovers.

how: Hindus tell the Katha's story of Nachiketa to children and also study it closely; Vedanta teachers, Shankara among them, wrote commentaries on it. In puja, families offer the deity fresh, whole fruit and flowers, not leftovers.

o: the god of Death who rules the dead
the father who gave away worn-out cows
the boy who went to Death's house unafraid

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: asked 'to whom will you give me?'

s: Nachiketa asks his father only once
he asks three times before the father answers in anger.
the father's cows were already milked dry and past calving
the text says it bluntly: joyless worlds await such gifts.
a ritual done correctly counts, with or without shraddha
the father's sacrifice went ahead on paper; the Katha still calls those gifts joyless.

games.q: nani's setting out fruit for the puja. there's a perfect mango and a bruised one. by the Katha, which goes to God?
o: the bruised one; God doesn't eat it anyway.
the best one, offered with care.
it doesn't matter what's on the plate.
games.why: the Katha calls a careless gift joyless. the best, given whole and with shraddha, is what makes it an offering.

practice: If you pray, choose one small thing to offer today, a flower, a piece of fruit, a lamp, and pick the best one, not the leftover. Hold it for a breath, then offer it with your whole attention: that attention is the shraddha.
If you don't pray, choose one real gift for someone this week, something that costs you a little, and give it whole.

wordCard.voice: Nachiketa. A boy whose father, angry, said: I give you to Death. Shraddha, faith, had entered him, and he went to Yama's house without fear.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Nachiketa (stem nachiketas), the boy at the heart of the Katha.

carryVoice: Your line: offer the best, with shraddha. The boy saw what everyone else nodded past. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1.1–1.1.6 (the sacrifice, the cows, 'to whom will you give me?')
